title: The Iterative Design Process
description: The stages of the iterative (cyclic) design process — design, make and evaluate — and the activities carried out.
content_html:
A Cyclic Approach to Design

The iterative design process is the cyclic, step-by-step framework through which most engineering design projects progress. Unlike linear design, the process loops back: after evaluating a prototype, the designer returns to the design stage to improve it, then makes and evaluates again. OCR R038 structures the iterative process into two main stages — Design and Make and Evaluate — each containing several distinct activities that you must be able to describe.

Stage 1 — Design: Analysing the Brief

Every iterative cycle begins with a thorough analysis of the design brief. The designer reads the brief carefully to identify what the product must do, who will use it, any constraints (cost, size, materials), and what success looks like. This analysis informs every later decision — if the brief is misunderstood, the entire cycle produces a product that fails to meet the client's needs.

Stage 1 — Design: Researching Product Requirements

Once the brief is understood, the designer researches what the product must achieve. Research falls into two types. Primary research gathers first-hand information from direct sources — interviews with potential users, focus groups, user observations, and the use of tables of anthropometric data to understand body dimensions. The advantage of primary research is that it is specific to the product; the disadvantage is that it is time-consuming and expensive to gather.

Secondary research uses existing published information — books, design guides, technical standards, and market research reports. Analysing existing products is a key secondary research activity: the ACCESS FM framework (Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, Materials and Manufacturing) provides a structured checklist for evaluating a competitor or similar product. Product disassembly — physically taking apart an existing product — is a secondary research technique that reveals how it is constructed and what materials are used. Secondary research is faster and cheaper than primary research but may be out of date or not specific to the new product.

Key Fact

ACCESS FM stands for Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, Materials and Manufacturing. This framework is used both as a research tool (to analyse existing products) and as a structure for writing the design specification — the same nine criteria appear in Topic Area 2.1 as the types of criteria included in a specification.

Stage 1 — Design: The Engineering Design Specification

After research, the designer writes an engineering design specification. The specification converts the client's needs into precise, testable criteria — for example, specifying that a product must weigh no more than 500 g, withstand a force of 200 N, or be produced for under £15. The specification is used throughout the iterative cycle to check whether the design is progressing in the right direction.

Stage 1 — Design: Generating Design Ideas

With a specification in place, the designer generates ideas. At the start of the first cycle, generation means creating new concepts through sketching (freehand drawings showing proportions, features and materials) and modelling (physical mock-ups or virtual 3D models). In later iterations, generation refers to the modification or improvement of an existing design in response to evaluation feedback. The ability to move fluidly between sketching and modelling — and between first ideas and refined revisions — is central to the iterative approach.

Sketching is fast and cheap — a designer can explore ten different forms in the time it would take to build one physical model. It communicates concepts quickly to a client or colleague. However, sketching cannot reveal how a 3D object actually fits together or moves. Physical and virtual modelling fills this gap: a 3D CAD model allows the designer to check proportions, spot interference between components, and simulate function before any material is cut. Both techniques complement each other, and in a thorough iterative process, ideas move between sketch and model multiple times before becoming a prototype.

Stage 2 — Make and Evaluate: Modelling

The make-and-evaluate stage begins with modelling. Models are made before a final prototype to test specific aspects of the design without the full cost of manufacture. The reasons for modelling are to test proportions (does the product look and feel the right size?), to test scale (does it fit the intended space or the user's hand?), and to test function (does it move, connect or operate as intended?).

Modelling takes two forms. Virtual modelling uses CAD software to create a digital representation; this allows dimensions to be checked, components to be assembled on screen, and simulations of stress or movement to be run — all before any physical material is used. Physical modelling creates a tangible object from card, foam, clay or other cheap materials; this allows the designer to assess ergonomics, user interaction and aesthetics in a way that a screen image cannot replicate.

Key Fact

Modelling is carried out to test three things: proportions, scale and function. Virtual modelling uses CAD software; physical modelling uses materials such as card, foam or clay. The distinction between virtual and physical modelling — and the specific things each can test — is directly examinable in R038.

Stage 2 — Make and Evaluate: Manufacture and Comparison

After modelling, the designer manufactures or modifies a prototype — a working version of the product built to check whether it meets the brief and specification. The prototype is then evaluated: its dimensions, function and quality are compared against the requirements of the design brief and specification. Where the prototype falls short, the cycle restarts — the designer returns to the design stage, modifies the idea, and makes a revised prototype. This loop continues until the product meets all specification criteria or until the project constraints (time or budget) require a final decision.

A model is made to test specific aspects of a design (proportions, scale, function) before committing to full manufacture — it is often not the same size, material or finish as the final product. A prototype is a working version of the product that is evaluated against the full design brief and specification. The distinction matters in exam questions: if asked about modelling, focus on testing and exploration; if asked about prototyping, focus on comparison against the specification and the decision to iterate or finalise. Mixing up these terms suggests a surface-level understanding and will cost marks on evaluation questions.
exam_tip_html: Questions on the iterative design process often ask you to describe what happens at a particular stage — always include both the activity and its purpose. For example, do not just write "the designer does research"; write "the designer carries out primary research by interviewing potential users to gather first-hand data about the product's requirements, which is then used to write the design specification." Linking each activity to its outcome and to the next stage is what separates Secure from Mastering answers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The iterative design process has two main stages — Design (brief analysis, research, specification, idea generation) and Make and Evaluate (modelling, prototype manufacture, comparison against the brief) — and the cycle repeats until the product meets all requirements.
  • Primary research gathers first-hand data from users (including anthropometric data, interviews and focus groups); secondary research uses existing sources including ACCESS FM analysis of existing products and product disassembly.
  • Modelling is carried out to test proportions, scale and function, using either virtual (CAD) or physical methods, before a prototype is manufactured and compared against the design specification.

glossary_terms.definition: A document issued by a client that outlines the problem to be solved, the intended user, and any constraints such as budget or materials.
Research that gathers new, first-hand information directly from users or experiments, such as interviews, surveys, focus groups and user observations.
A detailed document that sets out the measurable criteria a product must meet, derived from the design brief and research; used to guide design decisions and evaluate outcomes.
A framework for analysing products or writing design specifications using nine criteria: Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, Materials and Manufacturing.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the purpose of a design brief?
A) A document listing the materials to be used during manufacture
B) A document issued by the client outlining the problem, the user and any constraints
C) A checklist used to evaluate a finished product against ACCESS FM criteria
D) A record of all changes made during the iterative cycle
practice_questions.marks: B) A document issued by the client outlining the problem, the user and any constraints [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two activities that are carried out during the Design stage of the iterative design process.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: analysis of the design brief / researching product requirements (primary or secondary) / production of an engineering design specification / generation of design ideas by sketching and modelling. Accept any two clearly distinct activities. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of using primary research over secondary research when gathering information for a new product.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage (e.g. 'primary research is specific to the product'). 2 marks for development (e.g. 'because it collects first-hand data directly from the intended users, so the information reflects their actual needs rather than a generalised or outdated source'). 3 marks for a fully developed explanation with an applied example (e.g. 'for example, interviewing potential users of a new ergonomic tool reveals exactly how and where they hold it, which anthropometric data tables alone could not provide'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the term 'modelling' in the iterative design process. Give one example of a reason why a designer would make a model before manufacturing a prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): modelling involves creating a representation of the design — either virtual (using CAD software) or physical (using cheap materials such as card or foam) — to test specific aspects of the design without the full cost of manufacture (2 marks for a clear, developed description covering both types; 1 mark for a basic statement about making a model).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a designer might create a physical card model of a handheld device to test whether the proportions feel comfortable in the user's hand before committing to expensive tooling (2 marks for a specific, well-explained reason; 1 mark for a vague reason). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A design team is using the iterative design process to develop a new type of adjustable bicycle helmet. They have completed one cycle of design, make and evaluate, and the prototype does not fully meet the design specification.

Discuss what the team should do next and why the iterative process is beneficial in this situation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion explaining that the team should return to the design stage, analyse the evaluation feedback, modify the design ideas, produce a revised model and then a new prototype, and compare against the specification again. The discussion explains why iteration is beneficial (problems are caught and corrected progressively, reducing the risk of a flawed final product) and also acknowledges a limitation (additional cycles cost time and money, so there must be a point where the team commits to a final design). Both aspects are developed with reference to the helmet scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): The next steps are correctly identified and at least one benefit of iteration is explained with reference to the scenario, but the discussion may lack balance or depth.
Developing (2 marks): The idea of going back to the design stage is mentioned but not explained, or the benefit of iteration is stated but not developed.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A company designing a new children's educational toy has used both primary and secondary research during the Design stage of the iterative process.

Evaluate the extent to which a combination of primary and secondary research produces more useful information for writing a design specification than using only one type of research.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that clearly explains what each research type provides (primary: first-hand, product-specific user data from interviews, focus groups, anthropometrics; secondary: existing knowledge including ACCESS FM analysis of competing toys and market research), argues persuasively that combining both produces richer specification criteria (primary gives specific user insights; secondary gives broader context and saves time), and addresses the counter-argument (primary research alone might suffice if the user group is well-represented and resources are available; secondary alone might be adequate for a product in a well-documented market). A clear judgement is reached, supported by the educational toy context. Quality of written communication is high.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both research types are described accurately, reasons for using both are given with some application to the toy scenario, and an attempt at a judgement is made, but the counter-argument may be underdeveloped.
Developing (3–4 marks): Both research types are mentioned but mainly described rather than evaluated, or the argument is largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic description of one or both research types with little or no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What does the 'M' in ACCESS FM stand for when analysing an existing product?
Which of the following is an example of primary research in the iterative design process?
options: Conducting a focus group with potential users to identify their needs
Analysing a competitor product using ACCESS FM
Reading a published report on market trends
Studying a technical data sheet for a material

knowledge_checks.q: In the iterative design process, modelling is carried out to test proportions, _____, and function before committing to full prototype manufacture.
Product _____ is a secondary research technique where an existing product is physically taken apart to reveal how it is constructed and what materials are used.
Match each activity to the stage of the iterative design process in which it is carried out.
left: Carrying out focus groups with potential users
right: Design stage — researching product requirements (primary research)
Design stage — production of specification after research
Make and Evaluate stage — manufacture and comparison

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two main stages of the iterative design process?
flashcard_questions.a: The two main stages of the iterative design process are the Design stage and the Make and Evaluate stage, and the cycle repeats until the product meets the brief.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of analysing the design brief at the start of the iterative cycle?
flashcard_questions.a: Analysing the design brief allows the designer to identify what the product must do, who will use it, and any constraints such as budget or materials, which informs every.

flashcard_questions.q: What is primary research and give one example used in engineering design?
flashcard_questions.a: Primary research gathers first-hand information directly from users or experiments — one example in engineering design is conducting interviews with potential users to find out their specific needs and preferences.

flashcard_questions.q: What is secondary research and give one example used in engineering design?
flashcard_questions.a: Secondary research uses existing published information rather than gathering new data — one example in engineering design is using the ACCESS FM framework to analyse a competing product.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the nine headings of the ACCESS FM framework?
flashcard_questions.a: The nine headings of ACCESS FM are Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, Materials and Manufacturing — used both to analyse existing products and to structure a design specification.

flashcard_questions.q: What is product disassembly and why is it used as a research technique?
flashcard_questions.a: Product disassembly involves physically taking apart an existing product to reveal how it is constructed and what materials and manufacturing processes were used, giving insights that inform the new design.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an engineering design specification?
flashcard_questions.a: An engineering design specification is a document that sets out precise, measurable criteria the product must meet, derived from the brief and research, and used throughout the iterative cycle.

flashcard_questions.q: In idea generation, what is the difference between initial idea generation and generation in a later cycle?
flashcard_questions.a: In the first cycle, idea generation means creating completely new design concepts through sketching and modelling; in later cycles it means modifying and improving the existing design in response.

flashcard_questions.q: State three reasons why a designer makes a model during the iterative process.
flashcard_questions.a: A designer makes a model to test the proportions of the design, to test its scale in relation to the user or environment, and to test whether it functions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between virtual modelling and physical modelling?
flashcard_questions.a: Virtual modelling uses CAD software to create a digital representation of the design, while physical modelling creates a tangible object from materials such as card or foam that the.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens after a prototype is manufactured in the Make and Evaluate stage?
flashcard_questions.a: After manufacture, the prototype is compared against the requirements of the design brief and specification — if it falls short, the designer returns to the Design stage to refine.

flashcard_questions.q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of secondary research compared to primary research.
flashcard_questions.a: Secondary research is faster and cheaper to gather than primary research, but it may be out of date or not specific enough to the new product's exact requirements.
